strings.IRQ_THENEWORDER_DESC: Iraq is a curious case among the motley despots and colonialists within the Italian sphere. As the Italian attempt to integrate it as a puppet state of the empire failed miserably after a revolution, Rome was forced to accept Baghdad's autonomy, and Iraq is now one of the few truly democratic states in the Middle East, at least nominally. It operates as an authoritarian democracy, in which every willing political party under the sun is allowed a foot in the government so long as they don't challenge Italian control over the nation's oil, or the political dominance of Abd al-Karim Qasim and the National Democratic Party. But the system is a house of cards, with schemers, conspirators and plotters from every direction threatening Iraq and its leader. If (or when) it all comes tumbling down, who will rise from the ashes?
strings.IRQ_july_14_legacy_desc: It has been almost 5 years since the 14th July Revolution, and in many ways it remains unfinished. The revolution began as a popular and widespread uprising against Italian Influence, but rapidly devolved into anarchy, a war of all against all. Communists fought Shiites, democrats fought militarists, and everyone fought the Ba'athists. It was only the military coup of General Abd al-Karim Qasim and the forging of his government of national consensus that brought an end to the fighting. Since then, Qasim has been recognized by every party as Iraq's leader, but not a very powerful one. His rule is based on consensus, that the nation's factitious political parties are individually too weak to unite against him, and that the Italians will be forever desperate to support his regime as a bulwark against German-backed Ba'athism.
strings.IRQ_dawa_ascendant_desc: Much of the political scene in Iraq has been constant for decades. A weak puppet government supported by a foreign power. Pan-Arabists, numerous in their support but opposed by all others. Old men doddering about democracy, young men preaching communism. Opportunists and corruption in the army (and everywhere else). However, inspired by Iraq's economic stagnation and the oppression (both real and perceived) of their faith across the Middle East, Iraq's Shiites are flocking in ever greater numbers to join the Islamist Dawa Party, founded to represent them and their greivances. While the party itself is far from united, its star continues to rise even as Iraq's stability remains questionable, and few can doubt it's not a force to be reckoned with.
strings.IRQ_italian_interference_desc: While, on paper, Iraq is arguably the most independent nation of the Italian sphere, in reality the nation remains heavily dependent on its patrons in Rome. Iraq's oil is extracted by the Italians, its army is augmented and trained by Italian advisors, and its politics hampered by humiliating treaties which keep the nation limp wristed and dependent. While politicians of every stripe decry their nation's persistent servility, too many of them benefit too much from Italian patronage and corruption to do much about it.

strings.IRQ_ineffecient_oil_industry_desc: One would think that the discovery of massive oil reserves would lead to some sort of economic improvement. One would be surprised then, if they visited Iraq. Although Iraq's deserts are home to towering oil fields and its cities stuffed with refineries for the black gold, its actual production remains under par. What oil is produced is often stolen and sold on the black market, or lost somewhere in Iraq's maze of bureaucracy, cronyism, and pollution. If, against all odds, a barrel actually makes it to shipment, the money will mostly go to the Italians who ship it. Should a spare coin or two find its way back into the nation of its inception, then it will quickly go to line the pockets of the political or economic elite rather than into the hands of anyone who actually found the oil, extracted it, or worked to purify it.
strings.IRQ_the_spectre_of_baathism_desc: As elsewhere in the region, Iraq's Arabs grow increasingly restless, desiring a unified state, free from imperialism and western degeneracy. This is nothing new, and these feelings have been unleashed before, in the July 14th revolution (which drew its inspiration from the uprisings in Egypt and elsewhere). However, the revolution's failure did not defeat Iraqi Pan-Arabism, but instead made it clandestine, efficient, and highly organized through the Ba'ath party. While one might not be able to see the Ba'aths they are there nonetheless. Their posters appear at night despite the government's and garrison's dual efforts to remove them; their slogans are shouted at ever more common protests; and the desert seems to have an inexhaustible supply of these dedicated, angry men, hungry for the power they're sure will inevitably come their way.
strings.IRQ_MONEY_OUT_IRQ: We will Qasim's regime some money.
strings.IRQ_MONEY_IN_IRQ: Qasim's regime has paid us a shiny profit.
